reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ACR-EULAR
clinicalPearls: A systemic autoinflammatory disorder classically presenting with high spiking (quotidian) fevers, an evanescent salmon-pink rash, and arthritis or arthralgia
The rash is typically transient, appearing with fever spikes and fading between them
Sore throat is a common and underappreciated early feature
Laboratory findings include striking neutrophilic leucocytosis and very high serum ferritin, often with a low glycosylated (fraction) ferritin
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring careful search for infection, malignancy (especially lymphoma), and other autoimmune disease
Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies are characteristically negative
Macrophage activation syndrome (haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis) is a feared, potentially fatal complication
Management principles use NSAIDs for mild disease, corticosteroids for systemic disease, and IL-1 or IL-6 targeted biologics for refractory or relapsing cases
reference.pathophysiology: Adult-onset Still's disease is an autoinflammatory condition driven predominantly by innate immune activation rather than autoantibodies. Excessive activation of macrophages and neutrophils and a cytokine storm involving interleukin-1, interleukin-6, interleukin-18, and interferon-gamma produce the systemic inflammatory picture. Marked hyperferritinaemia reflects macrophage activation. Uncontrolled activation of macrophages and cytotoxic dysfunction can precipitate macrophage activation syndrome, characterised by cytopenias, coagulopathy, liver dysfunction, and extreme hyperferritinaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Sepsis and occult infection (including endocarditis and viral illness)
Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count (neutrophilic leucocytosis), inflammatory markers, and liver function tests
Serum ferritin, including glycosylated ferritin fraction where available
Extensive exclusion of infection (cultures, serology) and malignancy (imaging, marrow or node biopsy as indicated)
Autoantibody panel (rheumatoid factor and ANA, expected negative)
Monitoring for macrophage activation syndrome with triglycerides, fibrinogen, and evidence of haemophagocytosis
redFlags: Features of macrophage activation syndrome: persistent fever, cytopenias, falling fibrinogen, rising ferritin, and organ dysfunction
Haemodynamic instability or evidence of overwhelming infection mimicking the presentation
Fulminant hepatic involvement or disseminated intravascular coagulation
New lymphadenopathy or organomegaly raising concern for lymphoma
Cardiopulmonary complications such as myocarditis, pericarditis, or pleuritis
reference.prognosis: Course is variable, described as monocyclic (self-limiting), polycyclic (relapsing), or chronic articular with persistent destructive arthritis. Most systemic cases respond to treatment, but macrophage activation syndrome carries substantial mortality and requires prompt recognition and intensive therapy.
pitfalls: Anchoring on Still's disease before adequately excluding infection and malignancy
Missing early macrophage activation syndrome when a paradoxically falling ESR or ferritin trend is misread
Discounting the diagnosis because autoantibodies are negative (they are expected to be)
Overlooking sore throat and the transient rash as diagnostic clues
Failing to monitor for chronic destructive arthritis in the articular subtype
